file: papers/pdf/Graebner - 2004 - Momentum and Serendipity How Acquired Leaders Create Value in the Integration of Technology Firms.pdf
about: A grounded multiple-case study of eight technology venture acquisitions showing that acquired leaders create expected value through momentum-preserving actions and serendipitous (unanticipated) value through cross-organizational responsibilities.

candidates.label: Serendipitous value as unanticipated windfall
candidates.definition: Value or benefits that were not anticipated by the buyer before the deal; surprise gains that by definition come from an unexpected direction.
candidates.applies_when: An account describes a benefit or gain that the parties say they had not planned for or expected when entering the deal or venture.
candidates.does_not_apply_when: The benefit was the motive for the deal (expected value), even if it was exceeded; overshooting a planned target is not serendipitous.

candidates.label: Expected vs serendipitous value as independent
candidates.definition: Performance has two independent dimensions: expected value (benefits that motivated the deal) and serendipitous value; a firm can succeed on one and fail on the other.
candidates.applies_when: An account separates planned outcomes from unplanned gains, or notes unexpected gains despite failure on planned goals (or vice versa).

candidates.label: Serendipitous managerial/strategic value
candidates.definition: Unexpected gains in strategy or management, such as new strategic directions, new sales channels, revitalized marketing, or identifying new acquisition targets.
candidates.applies_when: Someone describes an unplanned strategic idea, new market approach, or management improvement arising from the combination.
candidates.does_not_apply_when: The gain is a technology or product-development technique (technological serendipitous value).

candidates.label: Serendipitous technological value
candidates.definition: Unexpected technological gains, such as discovering superior product development processes or unexpectedly useful technologies, arising when engineers from both firms share work.
candidates.applies_when: An account reports unexpected learning about technology or development processes through joint engineering work.

candidates.label: Cross-organizational responsibilities
candidates.definition: Serendipitous value emerges when acquired personnel are given tasks or roles spanning both the acquired and acquiring firms, either senior management over both or shared technical work.
candidates.applies_when: A person describes holding a role or task that spans both organizations and through it finding new opportunities.
candidates.does_not_apply_when: High-status positions that do not span both organizations; the author notes these may aid retention but need not lead to serendipitous value.

candidates.label: Exposure enables spotting opportunities
candidates.definition: Cross-organizational roles give acquired leaders visibility into the other firm's activities, letting them use their unique experience and information to spot unanticipated opportunities for value creation.
candidates.applies_when: Someone describes seeing a new opportunity because their position gave them a view into another organization's activities combined with their own knowledge.

candidates.label: Status/authority to bring discoveries to fruition
candidates.definition: Acquired personnel interacting from equal or higher status can have their ideas heard and executed, turning a discovered synergy into realized value.
candidates.applies_when: An account notes that a person's authority or peer standing allowed their unexpected idea to be adopted or implemented.
candidates.does_not_apply_when: The idea is spotted but ignored for lack of standing (see unrealized serendipitous potential).

candidates.label: Unanticipated resource recombination
candidates.definition: Serendipitous value is created by identifying opportunities for unexpected reconfiguration or recombination of the two firms' resources, unlike planned synergies that recombine resources predictably.
candidates.applies_when: An account describes combining resources (e.g., a sales force with another firm's product) in a way nobody had planned.
candidates.does_not_apply_when: Recombination that was the planned purpose of the deal.

candidates.label: Unique experience and informal relationships
candidates.definition: Acquired leaders draw on their own expertise and a broad, unusual combination of formal roles and informal relationships across organizations to leverage competencies across domains.
candidates.applies_when: Someone attributes a discovery to their prior industry knowledge or to relationships spanning organizations (e.g., knowing a startup the buyer did not).

candidates.label: Redirecting strategy of the combined firm
candidates.definition: Serendipitous insights can redirect the venture, e.g., dropping planned product development in favor of acquiring another start-up or entering a new customer segment.
candidates.applies_when: An account describes an unexpected insight changing the firm's direction, product plans, or target market.

candidates.label: Opened eyes to new markets and ideas
candidates.definition: Serendipitous discoveries reveal opportunities the firm was missing, such as new sales channels, better processes, or revitalized functions.
candidates.applies_when: People describe having their eyes opened, learning something new from partners, or a problem area being unexpectedly fixed.

candidates.label: Exploration beyond planned synergies
candidates.definition: Serendipitous value represents a more pronounced form of exploration involving entirely unanticipated recombinations, allowing exploration and exploitation to coexist.
candidates.applies_when: An account frames unexpected gains as genuinely new directions alongside ongoing execution of planned work.

candidates.label: Isolation blocks serendipity
candidates.definition: When acquired leaders are denied roles and engineers are kept isolated, potential serendipitous value is never realized and advice goes unheeded.
candidates.applies_when: An account describes recognized potential or offered ideas that went nowhere because the person was isolated or lacked access to decision makers.

candidates.label: Management vacancies and early deals
candidates.definition: Cross-organizational roles, and hence serendipity, are more likely when the buyer has open top-management positions, typical of its first few acquisitions; later acquirees find slots filled.
candidates.applies_when: Someone got a spanning role because of an unfilled position or because they were early, enabling unexpected contributions.

candidates.label: Structural pre-definition precludes serendipity
candidates.definition: Solutions that predefine where innovation should happen (e.g., dedicated units) would not foster serendipitous discoveries, since these come from unexpected directions; flexible cross-organizational exposure is needed.
candidates.applies_when: An account contrasts planned, designated innovation channels with discoveries arising from open, unplanned interaction.

candidates.label: Described as fortuitous after the fact
candidates.definition: Participants retrospectively describe decisions made for other reasons (e.g., desperation hires, keeping an employee) as turning out fortuitous.
candidates.applies_when: A narrator says a choice made reluctantly or for unrelated reasons 'turned out' to be lucky or highly valuable.

candidates.label: Richer resources explain windfalls
candidates.definition: An alternative hypothesis that acquired firms with more resources or experienced management simply yield more windfalls; the author argues cross-organizational roles also matter.
candidates.applies_when: An account attributes unexpected gains to the firm's inherent quality, resources, or experienced team rather than to positions enabling discovery.
